item.text: {"question_id":"6B.1","answer":"During López Obrador’s 2018–2023 administration, welfare was a genuine stated governing purpose, expressed through “Primero los pobres,” expanded social programs, constitutionalized senior pensions, and rights-oriented federal health rules. The administration also allocated substantial resources: the 2023 social-program budget rose 16.2% nominally, priority-program budgets rose 28.1%, and the older-adult pension had expanded by 2022 to 10.8 million recipients with reported exercised spending of 244,582.5 million pesos. Some 2023 operational evidence exists: Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro required monthly evaluations and workplace verification, though its reported performance was not independently audited. However, the evidence does not establish that all 2023 allocations were executed or that welfare commitments were broadly delivered. The policy record is materially mixed: health-access deprivation rose from 16.2% to 39.1% between 2018 and 2022, the health-and-medicines program’s real budget fell 35% from 2020 to 2023, and CONEVAL found that only 69% of priority programs had results orientation, 50% effectively measured results, and 38% showed logical linkage between components and objectives. Universalization also shifted resources away from the poorest: AP reported the poorest group’s share of social spending falling from about 19% in 2018 to 6% in 2020, while extreme poverty increased by about 400,000 people; these distributional figures are incomplete for 2023. Aggregate outcomes remain only partly attributable to López Obrador because Congress, agencies, subnational governments, donors, remittances, wage changes, the pandemic, demographic change, and external conditions also mattered. The best-supported conclusion for the 2023 period is therefore a substantial but imperfectly targeted and incompletely implemented welfare priority, with formal commitments and significant resource allocation more clearly evidenced than comprehensive delivery or end-period welfare effects.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0038-E001","BATCH-0048-E014","BATCH-0049-E006","BATCH-0051-E001","BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0038-E005","BATCH-0052-E001","BATCH-0052-E010"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-E016","BATCH-0031-E015","BATCH-0032-E002","BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0050-E002","BATCH-0047-E004","BATCH-0052-E003","BATCH-0054-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Most outcome evidence ends in 2022 or earlier rather than measuring 2023 end-period welfare.","The 2023 budget evidence establishes allocations, not universal execution, service quality, or completed delivery.","The 2023 operational evidence is program-specific and partly government-reported; it does not establish portfolio-wide implementation.","Distributional evidence is incomplete because the cited AP reporting notes that a 2022 distribution report was not published.","Causal attribution for national poverty, health, and deprivation outcomes is limited by pandemic effects, remittances, wage changes, demographic change, subnational and agency roles, and measurement limitations.","The supplied evidence does not establish a complete 2023 assessment of enforceability, political neutrality, or remedies across welfare programs."],"corrections_made":["Replaced the unsupported claim that the 2023 commitments were broadly “funded and partly implemented” with the narrower conclusion that they were formally funded or budgeted, with implementation demonstrated only for specified programs and prior-year pension spending.","Added the supplied contrary evidence on the 35% real decline in the health-and-medicines program budget, unclear health targeting, and the 69%/50%/38% program-quality findings.","Distinguished declared priorities, formal rules, budget allocations, executed prior-year spending, program operation, and outcomes.","Removed any implication that aggregate welfare outcomes establish direct presidential causation.","Retained the mixed distributional and health evidence, period fit, uncertainty, and incomplete 2023 outcome coverage."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["A full 2023 execution and incidence review could materially refine whether budgeted commitments translated into enforceable, equitable delivery.","Further evidence is needed on health-program implementation, service quality, appeals or remedies, and political neutrality across the portfolio.","The cited evidence supports a welfare orientation but does not by itself resolve whether universalization functioned primarily as broad social protection, political allocation, or a mixture."]}
